raw_record.support_text: The author notes that at the usual dosage Conteben is generally harmless to the liver, citing a fourth group of 15 pulmonary tuberculosis patients who, despite existing jaundice (interpreted as virus or homologous serum hepatitis), were able to continue the Conteben therapy begun before the jaundice appeared without worsening of the hepatitis. In paragraph 14 the author also states that the problem cannot be viewed in the sense that Conteben causes a parenchymal jaundice through sustained liver damage, and that the jaundice in these cases was no more severe than in non-Conteben-exposed patients from the same ward outbreak.
raw_record.extra_details: Support: 15 patients with pre-existing viral/serum hepatitis continued Conteben without worsening; jaundice episodes observed in a single prolonged-treatment case resolved without permanent liver damage (no lasting liver damage despite two intercurrent jaundice episodes). Author explicitly states Conteben does not cause parenchymal jaundice via sustained liver damage at ordinary dosage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude there is no clear causal relationship between desloratadine and the reported laboratory abnormalities, either through direct hepatotoxic effects or via CYP-based inhibition, and state they do not agree that all second-generation H1 blockers should be avoided in conjunction with azole antifungals.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-administration with azole antifungals in the reported critical-care case; causality disputed.

raw_record.support_text: Statement 25 in the guideline notes that methotrexate treatment is frequently associated with a slight increase in serum transaminases (up to 2-fold above the normal range), but states that this change is not predictive of significant liver toxicity and fibrosis and does not warrant drug discontinuation. This constitutes an explicit statement that these slight transaminase elevations do not represent clinically meaningful methotrexate-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Slight increase in serum transaminases up to 2-fold above normal is observed frequently during methotrexate therapy; explicitly stated not to predict significant liver toxicity or fibrosis and not to warrant drug discontinuation. Guideline statement (EL1 evidence level for the transaminase observation, EL4 for the management recommendation).

raw_record.support_text: The paper explicitly states that, unlike telcagepant, rimegepant does not cause liver damage during migraine use in the clinical setting, indicating the absence of a human DILI event for the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Claim refers to migraine clinical use (reference 52).
raw_record.extra_details: Rimegepant is a CGRP receptor antagonist used clinically for migraine; the paper states it does not cause liver damage in the clinical setting. Serial administration in mouse OA models also showed no liver adverse effects, but that is animal-only evidence and not counted here.

raw_record.support_text: According to this review, a variety of drugs have been reported to cause DRESS, a drug-induced multiorgan inflammatory response that characteristically includes hepatic dysfunction, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, sulfasalazine, NSAIDs, D-penicillamine, hydrochlorothiazide, cyclosporine, nevirapine, and allopurinol.
raw_record.extra_details: Cyclosporine is listed as reported to cause DRESS. Hepatic dysfunction is one of the internal-organ manifestations of the syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The paper repeatedly refers to acetaminophen-induced liver injury (AILI) in human patients. It states that in human DILI cases, serum miR-192 was substantially increased and miR-218 were moderately enhanced only in AILI patients and not in those who developed nonacetaminophen-induced liver injury. A separate human study found that a therapeutic dose of acetaminophen induced small alterations of 11 blood miRNAs in healthy subjects, possibly due to subtle toxicity not detectable by ALT, and the authors concluded that the miRNA changes were associated with liver injury after acetaminophen challenge rather than its pharmacological actions.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-induced liver injury (AILI) discussed throughout as a human DILI (paragraphs 26-30). In human DILI cases serum miR-192 was substantially increased and miR-218 moderately enhanced only in AILI patients, not in nonacetaminophen-induced liver injury or paraquat-induced liver injury. Nontoxic low-dose and toxic high-dose acetaminophen did not disrupt plasma miRNAs in mouse/rat/human when liver damage was not triggered, indicating miRNA changes were associated with liver injury rather than pharmacological effects; a therapeutic dose in healthy humans induced small alterations of 11 blood miRNAs possibly due to subtle toxicity not detectable by ALT. In the AILI animal model the injury features hepatocellular necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that inhibitors of (Na+,K+)-ATPase activity that predispose to, or induce, cholestasis are known, and explicitly names the antithyroid drugs carbimazole and methimazole among them. This is presented as a mechanism-based reference assertion that these agents cause cholestasis, in a review context focused on bile flow and membrane physiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited among inhibitors of (Na+,K+)-ATPase activity that are stated to predispose to, or induce, cholestasis (reference 15). Framed mechanistically in a review of cholestasis mechanisms; the paper also notes the experimental evidence linking (Na+,K+)-ATPase inhibition to cholestasis is partly conflicting.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that APAP (acetaminophen) is commonly used for pain and fever relief and is safe within therapeutic doses; however, at excessive doses it can cause severe hepatic toxicity and even acute liver failure. They further note that an overdose of APAP can initiate ferroptosis leading to significant liver damage, supporting the conclusion that APAP-induced damage involves eIF2α-ATF4 and ferroptosis activation. The experimental data in these paragraphs (lipid peroxidation, GPX4/CHAC1/SLC7A11/DDIT4/4-HNE changes, cell viability in AML12 and HepG2 cells) are cell-based mechanistic work.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; stated as safe within therapeutic doses, so injury is attributed specifically to excessive doses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP is described as safe at therapeutic doses but capable of causing severe hepatic toxicity and acute liver failure at excessive doses (cited ref 35). Overdose can initiate ferroptosis leading to significant liver damage (refs 36-37). The bulk of the presented evidence is in vitro/in vivo mechanistic work (AML12 and HepG2 cells, AML12/murine hepatocyte and C57BL/6 mouse models, GSE104601 human primary hepatocyte and PRJNA744757 datasets) on eIF2α-ATF4-mediated ferroptosis and its inhibition by 2BAct and Fer-1, which does not by itself constitute a distinct human DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: Two weeks after starting propylthiouracil (200 mg/day in 3 divided doses), the patient again developed asthenia, conjunctival jaundice, pruritus and dark urine; laboratory tests showed bilirubin 7 mg/dl (direct 5.5 mg/dl), GOT 135 U/l, GPT 448 U/l, GGT 357 U/l and alkaline phosphatase 279 U/l. This recurred after the patient had been warned about possible recurrent and potentially severe hepatotoxicity from another antithyroid drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy changed to propylthiouracil after methimazole-related hepatotoxicity in a Graves disease patient; recurrence of a similar liver reaction two weeks after starting PTU.
raw_record.extra_details: Graves disease patient; propylthiouracil 200 mg/day in 3 divided doses after prior methimazole-induced hepatotoxicity and after a warning about possible new and severe hepatotoxicity. Recurrence at ~2 weeks with asthenia, conjunctival jaundice, pruritus, dark urine; bilirubin 7 mg/dl (direct 5.5 mg/dl), GOT 135 U/l, GPT 448 U/l, GGT 357 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 279 U/l.

raw_record.support_text: In discussing treatment options for refractory macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), the paper states that etoposide, a key chemotherapeutic for HLH that inhibits topoisomerase II and suppresses inflammatory cytokine production, may cause severe side effects including severe bone marrow suppression as well as hepatic and renal toxicity, and cites an expert opinion favoring additional immunosuppressive agents rather than etoposide-containing HLH-specific therapy in patients with inadequate response to high-dose glucocorticoids.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Claim made in the setting of etoposide use for treatment of refractory MAS/HLH; coexistence of bone marrow and renal toxicity noted.
raw_record.extra_details: Etoposide is a topoisomerase II inhibitor used for HLH; hepatic toxicity is listed among potential severe side effects alongside severe bone marrow suppression and renal toxicity; an expert opinion suggested using additional immunosuppressive agents rather than etoposide-containing HLH-specific therapy. This is an assertion without primary patient data presented.

raw_record.support_text: The review states that long-term intake of iron supplements or some diseases may lead to chronic iron overload, and that when the binding capacity of transferrin is overwhelmed, accumulation of free iron in tissues results in damage of the liver, pancreas, heart, and other organs. Cirrhosis is listed among the symptoms of iron intoxication, along with heart failure, anemia, and arthritis. Separately (paragraph 82), hepatocellular necrosis and carcinoma are described as possible outcomes of iron overload, with dietary carbonyl iron shown to cause hepatic mitochondrial lipid peroxidation in rats.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term iron supplementation is only one route to iron overload; disease states and multiple blood transfusions are presented as additional causes. The claim merges general iron-toxicity pathology rather than a drug-specific DILI attribution, and the hepatocellular-necrosis/carcinoma outcome is supported in part by mechanistic and rat (dietary carbonyl iron) evidence.
raw_record.extra_details: Male free iron accumulates only when transferrin binding capacity is overwhelmed; the review notes iron toxicity is often overlooked relative to iron deficiency and lists iron intoxication symptoms as heart failure, cirrhosis, anemia, and arthritis. Hepatic outcomes of overload include mitochondrial swelling and rupture, hepatocellular necrosis and carcinoma attributed to free radical peroxidative reactions; carcinoma is non-neoplastic-excluded.

raw_record.support_text: Using signal mining on the FAERS database, the study identified adverse event signals connected to bedaquiline (BDQ). In addition to typical side effects (prolonged QT interval, vomiting, hepatotoxicity) from the package insert, the authors emphasize that male patients receiving bedaquiline for tuberculosis require stringent liver function monitoring to mitigate the risk of severe hepatotoxicity, and note that investigating the mechanisms of BDQ-induced liver injury, particularly involving the PI3K/Akt pathway, could inform future research.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings emphasized for male patients receiving bedaquiline therapy for tuberculosis.
raw_record.extra_details: FAERS database signal-mining study. Hepatotoxicity is listed among typical/package-insert side effects alongside prolonged QT interval and vomiting. Study discusses BDQ-induced liver injury involving the PI3K/Akt pathway as a proposed mechanism. No enzyme values, R ratio, latency, case counts, or formal causality instrument scores are provided in the available text.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity after acute overdose is well documented in the literature, with more severe signs including hepatic damage. In the reported case a 28-year-old man intentionally ingested up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets) plus an unknown quantity of ibuprofen and developed acute renal and fulminant liver failure; his admission acetaminophen level was 316 µg/ml and liver tests were markedly elevated (AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, INR 5.3), and he underwent liver transplantation on hospital day 3.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-ingestion of an unknown quantity of ibuprofen during the intentional overdose; patient had schizophrenia.
raw_record.extra_details: Intentional overdose of up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets); admission acetaminophen level 316 µg/ml (critical value > 40 µg/ml); treated with IV acetylcysteine; acute renal and fulminant liver failure; AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, INR 5.3, pH 6.9, lactic acid 13.7 mEq/L; liver transplantation on day 3 with necrotic bowel found at surgery; rhabdomyolysis was a rare co-occurrence and the Naranjo scale indicated a probable acetaminophen-overdose-associated reaction for rhabdomyolysis; the literature does not clearly associate acetaminophen with rhabdomyolysis because of other possible causes.

raw_record.support_text: In a large psychiatric hospital, nine patients with chlorpromazine jaundice (allergic cholangiolitis following administration of chlorpromazine) were studied in sufficient detail to warrant inclusion in the report; the authors state that liver cell damage is usual in this disease. They underwent intensive serial clinical, laboratory, and serial needle aspiration biopsy studies, documenting chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic liver injury with associated liver cell degeneration.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine psychiatric inpatients with chlorpromazine jaundice; 26 percutaneous needle aspiration biopsies. Histology showed liver cell damage typical of the disease: ballooning degeneration of liver cells, multinucleation, mitoses, unicellular and periportal focal necroses with Councilman-like bodies, and one fatal literature case (Rodin and Robertson) with diffuse non-inflammatory centrolobular necroses preserved supporting reticulum (feathery necrosis). Features of allergic cholangiolitis: jaundice, bile in urine, elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (Bodansky units) and cholesterol, eosinophilia; all nine present cases recovered, though some laboratory abnormalities persisted for months.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that their patient had elevations in liver enzymes after losartan use which returned to normal after discontinuation, re-elevations after rechallenge, no evidence of other hepatic disorders, a biopsy consistent with hepatic damage, and normal liver tests during a 2-year follow-up, and that these data clearly demonstrate the existence of losartan-induced hepatic injury in this patient. The majority of drug-related reactions are described as idiosyncratic and unpredictable.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old female treated with losartan 50 mg/d for 5 months; AST rose to 1,093 U/L, ALT 941 U/L, total bilirubin 8.9 mg/dL after rechallenge; liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with a mild-severe inflammatory response and mild fibrosis; enzymes normalized after discontinuation and rechallenge reproduced the injury; 2-year follow-up normal with recovery. A compiled table summarizes 5 reported cases of losartan-induced hepatic injury (additional prior cases from refs 7-9), all of whom improved.

raw_record.support_text: The mechanism of ticlopidine-induced hepatic injury remains unknown; immune mechanisms, drug hypersensitivity, or direct toxicity of ticlopidine or one of its metabolites have been proposed. Differences in metabolic pathways or rate in different individuals may be the basis for the idiosyncratic nature of ticlopidine-induced cholestasis. In vitro proliferation studies may support a T-cell-mediated mechanism for ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis, and transient eosinophilia in patients favors an immune rather than toxic mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis with histology showing either cholestasis or a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular damage pattern, plus mononuclear or mononuclear/neutrophilic portal infiltrates. The paper proposes immune/hypersensitivity and possibly direct toxicity mechanisms, and notes the idiosyncratic nature of ticlopidine-induced cholestasis. Upon discontinuation symptoms usually resolved within 1-3 months, though cholestasis could last >6 months and in 2 cases >1 year; there were no fatal cases and no irreversible hepatic damage, the only reported fatal case being due to co-occurring neutropenia leading to septic shock. Ticlopidine is an antiplatelet thienopyridine. The paper is a case series/review combining literature cases and the authors' own patients.
